memory_text: ## 2026-09-13 — speed graph, the channel evaluator, and a hole in the codegen gate (11.11) **The gap found first.** There was **no channel evaluator anywhere** — not in Rust, not in TypeScript. `SceneEasing` and `CubicBezier` were data with nothing that read them. So the speed graph had no curve to draw, and 11.24's playback would have had nothing to play. 11.11 had to build the evaluator before it could build the view. **Rust owns it.** `gx_contracts::animation` gained `ease_at`, `easing_control_points`, `evaluate_channel` and `evaluate_scene_at`. The solve is Newton-Raphson with a bisection fallback — the method browsers use for `cubic-bezier()`, and matching them is deliberate. Two decisions worth keeping: - **Outside the keyed range the value holds flat, never extrapolates.** Extrapolation invents motion nobody authored, which on air is a graphic drifting for no reason. - **`Hold` returns 0 progress**, which is what produces a step rather than a ramp; the next key takes over exactly at its own frame. **The mirror is pinned, following 11.4.** A browser cannot call Rust once per pixel, so the solve is mirrored in `Editor/src/timeline/easing.ts` and pinned against `Editor/src/easing-reference.ts`, which `gx-contract-codegen` generates **by running the Rust**.
